paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A heat wave, sometimes called extreme heat, is a stretch of unusually hot weather lasting several days. Heat is usually judged against the local climate and the normal temperatures for that time of year. So weather that people from a hot country think of as ordinary can be a heat wave in a cooler region, if it falls outside that region's normal pattern. The hard part of this broad definition is pinning down what normal means and how large an area the event must cover.

paragraphs.heading: How heat waves form
paragraphs.text: A heat wave builds when a high-pressure area high in the atmosphere grows stronger and sits over one region for days or even weeks. This holds the heat down near the ground. Forecasters can usually see heat waves coming, so officials can warn people ahead of time.

paragraphs.heading: Drawing the line
paragraphs.text: Several countries set their own thresholds. Sweden calls it a heat wave when the daily high tops 25 °C (77.0 °F) for at least five days running. Singapore needs an average daily maximum of at least 35 °C (95.0 °F) over three days in a row, with an average daily mean of 29 °C (84.2 °F) or more. Out at sea, scientists speak of marine heatwaves: long, distinct spells when the surface water in a region stays unusually warm.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Heat waves are a kind of extreme weather, and they endanger health because heat and sunshine can overwhelm the body's ability to control its own temperature. Severe ones have caused disastrous crop failures and thousands of deaths from hyperthermia. They raise the risk of wildfires where there is drought, and they can strain power grids enough to cause blackouts or brownouts. They also cost money, by lowering how much work people get done, disrupting farms and factories, and damaging infrastructure.

paragraphs.heading: A warming world
paragraphs.text: Since the 1950s, heat waves over land have grown more frequent and more intense across almost every part of the planet. Climate change is behind their rising frequency and longer duration. The World Meteorological Organization reported that heat waves kept getting stronger in 2024, with record temperatures in Europe, North America and China. In many regions the thermometer stayed above 45 °C (113 °F) for days on end.
